inline.s: Five: do not befriend kin and friends, answer invitations and gatherings, roam the hills and admire scenery, or pass idle
(leisure)
talk. Of all the countless affairs of worldly convention, apart from what rightful duty and necessity require and cannot be avoided, put all the rest aside, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Five: do not befriend kin and friends, answer invitations and other social engagements, roam the hills and admire scenery, or pass idle talk and chat. Of all the affairs of the world, apart from what right and duty require and cannot be declined, set the rest all aside, keeping a single-minded right thought.
Six: do not cling to ease and indulgence, giving free rein to sleep. While the great affair is not yet made clear, toil and bear hardship, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Six: do not be greedy and attached, giving free and easy rein to mind and body, and letting sleep run its course. Since the great affair is not yet clear, one must be diligent and bear hardship, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Seven: do not compete with the world in talent and ability, contend for fame and power, claim attainment when not attained, claim realization when not realized, deceive others into calling you a good friend of the Dharma, and vainly exalt yourself. One should only hold to humility and keep to ignorance, remaining all one's life in the position of a student, and discipline oneself, ever advancing diligently, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Seven: do not compete with the world in talent and ability, contend for fame and power, claim attainment when not attained, claim realization when not realized, falsely call yourself a good friend of the Dharma, and vainly exalt yourself. One should only hold to humility and keep to ignorance, remain all one's life in the position of a student, discipline oneself, and unceasingly make progress, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Wei de yan de, wei zheng yan zheng (claiming attainment when not attained, claiming realization when not realized): not having obtained the holy Dharma, yet saying one has obtained it; not having realized the fruit of the Way, yet saying one has realized it.

In the Qing dynasty there was an old woman known as "Care-About-Nothing"; we do not know her name, and know only that she was a native of Hangzhou. She once asked the monk Daoyuan of the Xiaoci Nunnery, "What practice should one cultivate to be certain of escaping the sea of suffering in this lifetime?" The monk Daoyuan answered, "Nothing surpasses reciting the Buddha's name. Yet reciting the Buddha's name is not hard; the difficulty lies in
lasting long
; lasting long is not hard, the difficulty lies in
single-mindedness

." If you can set aside all worldly affairs and single-mindedly hold the name and recite the Buddha, with sincere resolve to seek rebirth, then at death the Buddha will come to receive you, and you will escape the sea of suffering!" The old lady joyfully bowed in thanks. When she returned home she at once entrusted the household affairs to her daughters-in-law, set apart a pure chamber where she enshrined a Buddha image, and practiced within it.

After more than a year had passed, she came again to ask the monk Daoyuan: "Ever since receiving your instruction, your disciple has given up household affairs and applies herself with a single mind to reciting the Buddha's name. I can say of myself that I have been able to recite long without slackening, but I am tormented by the difficulty of single-mindedness and cannot attain it. Pray, master, teach me once more what to do." The monk Daoyuan said, "Although you have cast off the household affairs, you are still not without attachment to your sons, grandsons, and relatives. If this root of love is not pulled up, how can you attain single-mindedness? To advance a step further, you must first pull up the root of love, put down everything, and only then can you attain single-mindedness!" The old lady sighed, "How right the master is! Though my body no longer concerns itself, my mind has still not let go. From today on I truly will become a person who cares about nothing!" From then on she practiced all the more earnestly. When the thought of love stirred now and then, she would at once silently recite the three words "care about nothing" to drive it off. When she was asked about household affairs, she likewise refused with these three words. Thus the great name "Care-About-Nothing" spread among her relatives and through the village. In this way more than another year passed. One day she came to the Xiaoci Nunnery, bowed in thanks to Daoyuan, and said, "The master has not deceived me; your disciple is to travel West within a few days!" Several days later, she passed away without any illness.
The original text:

In the Qing dynasty, an old woman called Care-About-Nothing, whose surname is lost, was a native of Hangzhou. Once she asked the monk Daoyuan of Xiaoci Nunnery, "What practice should one cultivate to be certain of leaving the sea of suffering in this lifetime?" The monk said, "None surpasses reciting the Buddha's name. Yet reciting the name is not hard; what is hard is lasting long. Lasting long is not hard; what is hard is single-mindedness. If you can disregard everything, set your mind singly on holding the name, and with complete sincerity resolve to seek rebirth, then at death the Buddha will come to receive you and you will escape the sea of suffering." Joyfully she bowed in thanks. At once she entrusted her household affairs to her daughters-in-law and the like, set apart a pure chamber to enshrine the Buddha, and practiced within it. After more than a year she went again to ask him, saying, "Ever since receiving your instruction, your disciple has set aside household affairs and confined herself to reciting the Buddha's name. Of myself I can say that I have been able to recite long without slackening, but I am tormented by the difficulty of single-mindedness; the master must have something to teach me!" The monk said, "Though you have cast off household affairs, you are not without attachment to your sons, grandsons, and relations. This is the root of love not yet drawn out; how can you attain single-mindedness? Now make further effort, first drawing out the root of love and putting down everything; only then can you attain single-mindedness." Sighing, she said, "The master's words are right. Though I no longer concern my body, I cannot help but concern my mind; from today on I truly remain one who cares about nothing." So she pressed on all the more earnestly. When the thought of love stirred now and then, she silently held to the three words "care about nothing" to drive it away. When she was consulted about household affairs, she likewise refused with these three words. Thus the name Care-About-Nothing spread among her relations and friends. After another year she went to the nunnery to thank him, saying, "The master does not deceive me; your disciple's day to travel West is set." A few days later, she died without any illness.
(Recorded from the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.)

On New Year's Eve of the yichou year of the Jiajing era (1565), Master Zhuhong had his wife, Lady Tang, steep some tea. Lady Tang carried the tea to the table, and by a slip let it fall to the ground. When the master saw that his beloved ancestral jade cup was shattered, he smiled and said:
"There is no condition or karma that does not part."

The following year he took leave of Lady Tang, saying, "No affection or kindness can last forever, and in birth and death no one can stand in for another. I am going to leave the household life; arrange things well for yourself." Lady Tang, free and easy, said, "Go on ahead; once I have set the household affairs in order, I too will leave the household life." And so the master composed the lyric "Crossed Out at One Stroke" and left the household life.

Yi bi gou (to cross out at one stroke): this was an expression ancients used for settling accounts, meaning to blot out a settled debt with one stroke; later it was extended to mean canceling everything outright, wiping it all away in a single stroke. For instance, the Daoist Lu Dongbin of the late Tang, in his verse on awakening, "The Garden of Spring," said: "Rest, rest, turn your head in good time, and hook away with one stroke the gallantries of former days."

The debt of kindness weighs like mountains high; / the five cauldrons and three victims cannot all repay. / When parents reach release from the dust's defilement, / then the way of a child is fulfilled. / Ah! The great cause of leaving the world, / how can worldly feeling fathom this? / A filial son, a virtuous new descendant, / should seek well the true void. / Therefore cross out at one stroke the five-colored golden seal of rank.

The kindness of parents is heavy as great mountains; the five cauldrons and three victims would not suffice to repay it. Only by saving both parents to escape birth and death is the filial way of the child fulfilled. Ah! This great cause of leaving the world, how can the feelings and consciousness of the ordinary person comprehend it through and through? A true filial son and virtuous descendant should investigate the reality of all dharmas (for it is only by one's own attainment of the Way that one can save one's parents from the sea of birth and death); therefore cross out at one stroke the five-colored golden insignia of name-reflecting and ancestor-glorifying rank.

Wu ding san sheng (the five cauldrons and three victims): describes offerings of utmost abundance. Wu ding: in the ancient rites, a high official used five cauldrons. San sheng: ox, sheep, and pig. "Qin de li chen gou, zi dao fang cheng jiu" (when parents attain release from the dust, the way of the child is fulfilled): this means that only when parents escape birth and death (are free of the dust) has the child truly fulfilled filial piety. "Cha
cha

" an exclamation, here a blow struck on the head from the master. Zhen kong (true emptiness): the reality of all dharmas. Zhu fa shi xiang (the reality of all dharmas): the actual state of all things. The Buddha-Store Sutra says:
"What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing abiding."
(See in detail the
Reality of All Dharmas
article.)

Wu se jin zhang (the five-colored golden insignia): the robes of high officials in ancient times; here it refers to achieving fame and rank, reflecting honor upon parents, and glorifying one's ancestors.
Master Hanshan Deqing said:

"What all the world's parents hope of their children is that they be honored and make the family name shine, and so regard nourishing them with the three victims and five cauldrons as fulfilling filial piety. They little know that the richer the support, the deeper the suffering; this is to burden one's parents, not true filial piety. Therefore the World-Honored One, our Buddha, disdaining the golden wheel
(disdaining the station of a wheel-turning king)

and not taking it, abandoned his parents, left the king's palace, practiced austerities in the snow mountains, and after six years attained the Way, becoming the honored one of the three worlds, revered by gods and men. Had he not renounced the utmost honor and cut away the great love, how could he have won the undying karma of a long age of kalpas? Hence it is called: "Great is the filial piety of Shakyamuni, the Honored One, repaying his parents' kindness through kalpa after kalpa." Is this not taking the realization of the unborn and the universal salvation of beings as the ground of requital? The Buddha, in the great precepts, says first of all, "Filial piety is called the precept" — that is, to be filial to parents, filial to the teachers and the Three Jewels, filial to the supreme Way, and filial to all beings. Therefore one who truly studies and practices the Buddha's teaching will regard all beings as his parents in many former lives,
(how could one fail to repay even the kindness of this life's parents?)
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Exhortation to the Layman Wang Zijian on Relinquishing His Son to the Monastic Life.)

blocks.text: 2. The Chapter on Husband and Wife

inline.s: Phoenix mate and phoenix companion, / when will the tangle of love and kindness end? / Living ghosts in borrowed forms keeping each other company, / when the affinity is spent, still we must part. / Ah! For your two hearts so deeply entwined, / wearing the cangue and the shackles; / see through him who is your foe, / and each seek out a door to go. / Therefore cross out at one stroke the fish-and-water husband and wife.

Phoenix mate and phoenix companion, when will the tangle of love and kindness end? Are we not a pair of living ghosts in borrowed forms keeping each other company, and when the affinity is spent we still must part? Ah! For the sake of your two hearts so deeply entwined, we wear the cangue and the shackles and drift through the world. See through that you are a foe come to collect a debt, and each of you seek the door of liberation and go. Therefore cross out at one stroke the fish-and-water husband and wife.
Feng lü luan chou (phoenix mate and phoenix companion): refers to the love of man and woman, harmonious and companionable as the phoenix and the luan bird. "Chou
chou
": a kind of ancient shackle or manacle. "Chou mou
chou mou

": deep and long-lasting, the entangling of passion: two hearts enwrapped in love. Yuan jia (a foe): an adversary who comes to exact retribution. "Husband and wife are foes" means that each is dragging the other along, suffering endlessly in the cycle of birth and death. The Surangama Sutra says:
"You love my mind, I pity your beauty; by this cause and condition, through a hundred thousand kalpas, you are forever entangled."

The remedy is to enter the gate of liberation, passing from lovers to fellow practitioners. Ge zi xun men zou (each seeking his own door): each seeks the door of escaping birth and death (the Buddha's gate) and leaves.

blocks.text: 3. The Chapter on Sons and Grandsons

inline.s: The body is like a sore and a pustule
(you)

; do not grieve far ahead for your sons and grandsons. Recall the Dou of Yanshan, do they still live today? Ah! In the end there is a time of rest, and all comes to having no posterity. Who knows that the true self, through ten thousand ages, stays as old as ever? Therefore cross out at one stroke the cassia-branch and orchis-dark sons and grandsons.

The defiled and bitter physical body is like a sore and a pustule; do not grieve far ahead for your sons and grandsons. Recall the Dou of Yanshan who taught his five sons, and whose fame swept across the earth, are they still here today? Ah! In the end there is a time of rest, and all comes to having no posterity; upon the road of the Yellow Springs one walks alone. Who recognizes the true self (one's own nature), which through ten thousand ages is as old as ever (never aging, never dying)? Therefore cross out at one stroke the cassia-branch and orchis-dark sons and grandsons.

Yanshan Dou: that is, Dou Yujun, a man of the Later Jin era of the Five Dynasties. His ancestral home was Yuyang in Jizhou, in the region of the Yanshan mountains, so later generations respectfully called him the Dou of Yanshan, an ancient custom of honoring a person by naming his place. He governed his household with strict discipline and had five sons, all excellent in both learning and conduct, whom contemporaries praised as the "Five Dragons of Dou"; all passed the highest examinations and became pillars of the state. The Three Character Classic says, "Dou of Yanshan had righteous ways; he taught five sons, and their names were all made known." Jin ri huan cun fou (do they still survive today?): "Where are the generals and ministers, ancient and modern, today? A mound of withered graves, grass gone to nothing." (From the "Good-Bye Song" in Dream of the Red Chamber.) Zong gui wu hou (all comes to having no posterity): when one last breath stops, one walks alone on the Yellow Springs road; and, after all, what sons and grandsons are there?

Shui shi dang ren (who knows the very self): who is it that recognizes the self-nature as one's true self? Beings, in their delusion, falsely take this physical body as the self and do not recognize that the self-nature is the self; hence there is birth and death and transmigration. The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says:

"All sentient beings, from beginnings time, are turned upside down in all manner of ways, like a lost man who takes the four directions wrongly; they falsely take the four great elements as the self's body and the shadow-images of the six dusts as the self's mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the air and a second moon; from this false thinking they revolve in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance."

Translation: All sentient beings, from beginnings time, with their self-nature deluded and reversed, give rise to all manner of inverted views, taking the false as true. This is like one who has lost his way and takes north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the flesh-and-blood body, formed of earth, water, fire, and wind, as the self's body, and the discriminating mind that conditions upon the six dusts with the six faculties (the shadow-images of the six dusts) as the self's mind. It is like one with blurred vision who falsely sees flowers in the air and a second moon.

Because beings, in their inverted confusion, falsely take the body and mind, which are but illusions, as real and grasp them as a self, they revolve endlessly in birth and death; and so it is called ignorance.

Si da (the four great elements): the earth, water, fire, and wind elements. Earth is of the nature of solidity, water of wetness, fire of warmth, and wind of flowing. All the tangible matter of the world possesses these four natures of solidity, wetness, warmth, and movement, and so they are called "great." The physical body is composed of the four great elements; here "four great elements" refers to the physical body. Liu chen yuan ying (the shadow-images of the six dusts): the various thoughts produced when the six faculties condition upon the six dusts; since these thoughts are all false and insubstantial, they are called the shadow-images of the six dusts, the phantoms caused by conditioning on the six dusts. Gui zi lan sun (cassia-branch and orchis-dark sons and grandsons): a beautiful term for the descendants of others. When sons and grandsons are honored and prosperous together, it is called orchis and cassia blooming in harmony.

blocks.text: 4. The Chapter on Fame and Rank

inline.s: Standing alone at the ao's head, / say not that now is the season of a man's triumph. / The golden seal, hanging like a measure of grain, / its splendor is not to last long. / Ah! how many rush about in vain, / from rosy youth to hoary white hair. / Waking from the dream of yellow millet, / one laugh, and there is nothing at all. / Therefore cross out at one stroke wealth, honor, fame, and rank.

Standing alone at the ao's head, do not say it is the season of a man's pride. The golden seal, hanging pendulous, its splendor cannot last long. Ah! How many waste their efforts in vain, their rosy youth turning in a blink to hoary hair. The yellow-millet dream wakes, and what is there to show? Therefore cross out at one stroke wealth, honor, fame, and rank.

Du zhan ao tou (to stand alone at the ao's head): the "ao's head" is the relief of an ao-turtle on the steps before the palace gate; when the results of the imperial examination were posted, the top graduate stood upon it to receive the announcement. Sheng shi bing fei neng chang jiu (its splendor cannot last long): wealth and honor, brilliance and eloquence, and perfect happiness cannot endure forever. This is precisely why one crosses out at one stroke! If one does not cross it out oneself, impermanence will come to cross it out back, and at that time birth and death will not be in one's own control. Duo shao wang chi qiu (how many rush about in vain): "Where, today, are the generals and ministers of old? A mound of withered graves, grass gone to nothing." (From the "Good-Bye Song" in Dream of the Red Chamber.)
Huang liang yi meng (the dream of yellow millet): comes from the Tang dynasty work "The Tale of the Pillow":
"In the seventh year of the Kaicheng era there was a scholar named Lu, given name Ying, courtesy name Cuizhi. At an inn in Handan
(an inn)

, he met a Daoist elder named Lu. The scholar lamented deeply his poverty; the elder then took a pillow from his bag and gave it to him, saying, "If you rest your head upon this pillow of mine, you shall surely be honored, prosperous, and at ease!" At that time the host was just steaming millet
(yellow millet)

. The scholar bent his head to the pillow and fell asleep inside it, and so came to his own house. After some months he married a daughter of the Cui family of Qinghe. The lady was most beautiful, and her dowry
(dowry)
was the richer for it, and the scholar was greatly delighted. And so, soon
(before long)
he passed the highest examination, and rising in office (jilei) reached the rank of the Secretariat Drafter
(reaching by accumulated merit the rank of Secretariat Drafter)
; he was promoted to military governor
(promoted to military governor)
; he roundly defeated the barbarian tribes, and became prime minister
(becoming prime minister)
for more than ten years. His five sons all held office
(official posts)
, his grandsons were ten and more, and his marriage ties
(affinal relations)
were all with the most distinguished families of the empire
(eminent families)
; he lived past eighty and died
(zu, passed away)
. When he awoke, the millet had not yet finished steaming. Astonished
(amazed)
, he said, "Was it all a dream
(could this have been a dream?)
?" The elder laughed, "The satisfactions of life
(encounters and fortunes)
, are just like this!" The scholar, stunned and lost
(bewildered and self-forgetting)
for a long while, bowed his head in thanks and departed."
Huang liang: yellow millet. Ji yu (encounter): a meeting, usually a good one. Qi shou: to kneel, bring one's clasped hands to the ground, and lower the head also to the ground.
